newsitem.title: UK: Microprocessors still powering ahead after 25 yrs.
newsitem.headline: Microprocessors still powering ahead after 25 yrs.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Microprocessors, the brains of computers, will only improve with age, Intel Corp said on Friday at its press conference to celebrate the 25th anniversary of its invention.
Using silicon wafers with integrated transistors, microprocessors will continue to steadily increase in power while getting smaller and cheaper, Intel said.
"If current industry trends continue, microprocessors will become 10-fold faster and more powerful than they are today, facilitating an endless array of new applications," Intel said in a statement.
These types of visions for the microprocessor are a long way from 1971, when Intel's first microprocessor contained the equivalent of only two transistors.
Since then, the number of transistors has doubled about every two years, with each chip now containing 10,000 transistors. By 2000, each chip is expected grow to contain 100,000 transistors.
This exponential growth has led to a slashing of costs in personal computers (PCs).
In 1991, a PC cost about $6,200 and the cost of its data was the equivalent of $225 for each million instructions per second.
By 1995, a PC cost about $1,400 and cost of its performance was $11 for every million instruction per second, Intel said.
And the advent of the PC, in turn, was a boon to democracy, said Intel's Ted Hoff, father of the microprocessor.
"Information is power. I like the way the microprocessor has spread that power around," Hoff said.

The microprocessor's own extra power at cheaper prices also helped propel microprocessors into a huge range of everyday applications including consumer electronic games and appliances, engine management systems for cars, traffic light controllers, electronic musical instruments, cellular telephones and point of sale terminals in shops.
Hoff said his invention a quarter century ago helped move a room-full of equipment into a device the size of a fingertip.
And now, with an expected onward march of ever more powerful, smaller and cheaper microprocessors, the worlds of entertainment and communications are also within reach.

"At home, people will be able to view and print family photos from digital cameras. The increase in power will make them easier to use, allow voice and handwriting recognition and life-like animation," said Keith Chapple, managing director of Intel Corp UK.

In addition, he said "audio, video and conferencing capabilities will be integrated with the World Wide Web," which helps organise the mass of data available to people around the world via the Internet. The Internet is a growing, worldwide network of personal computers linked by telephone lines.
